I excused myself and threw up in the bathroom, then splashed cold water on my face until my hands stopped shaking.

The irony felt heavy on my chest, like I'd swallowed something that wouldn't go down. I wondered if he even remembered what he'd done. Probably not. People like him never did.

Jordan's laugh came out wrong, more like a cough. This was the same Tyler who'd made sure Jordan never felt safe at school, who'd turned "judgment" into an art form. Jordan closed the browser. He'd been feeling hollow for months now, moving through days like he was watching himself from somewhere far away, but apparently not hollow enough to sit across from Tyler Morrison and talk about his feelings. He ordered takeout he wouldn't eat and turned on the TV to fill the silence.

topic: A person learns their childhood bully became a therapist
story: The worst part was that Christina had probably become a good therapist. She'd always been perceptive—that's what had made her bullying so effective. The irony sat in Nina's throat like a stone. She'd been gathering courage for weeks to seek help, had finally admitted she couldn't keep feeling this way—this emptiness, this weight that made every task feel impossible. She'd finally accepted she needed support. And the best-reviewed therapist in her insurance network was Christina Hayes. Nina closed her laptop and climbed back into bed, still wearing yesterday's clothes. Maybe tomorrow. Maybe never.

topic: A person learns their childhood bully became a therapist
story: "You should really talk to someone," my roommate said, her voice gentle but worried. She'd found me sitting in the dark again, had noticed I'd stopped going to my classes. I nodded because it was easier than explaining that I'd tried. That I'd actually made an appointment with a highly recommended therapist. That I'd walked into the waiting room and seen, on the door, "Dr. Kevin Bradshaw." That I'd recognized the name immediately—the boy who'd tormented me for two whole years, who'd made me dread every school day. I'd turned around and left, told the receptionist I had the wrong office. Now I was back in my room, curtains drawn, trying to remember when everything had started feeling so heavy. The answer didn't matter. Nothing much seemed to matter anymore.

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:
Marcus stared at his coffee, watching the cream swirl without mixing. "Remember when we started the business? That night at the bar when we sketched everything on napkins?"

"Oh yeah," Derek laughed. "You were so nervous you could barely speak. I had to do all the talking to that investor guy."

Marcus's grip tightened on the mug. "That's... that's not how it happened. You were the one who froze up. I pitched the whole thing while you sat there."

"Dude, no. I remember it clearly—you were shaking."

The coffee had gone cold in Marcus's hands. He set it down and looked out the window, his reflection hollow in the glass. All these years, he'd held onto that memory as proof he was capable, that he'd been brave once. His throat felt thick. "Maybe you're right," he managed, though the words came out flat.

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:
I keep replaying it in my mind, but every time I do, Sarah's version creeps in and corrupts my own. We were talking about the day Mom died, something we never do. I told her how Mom squeezed my hand at the end, how she looked right at me and smiled. Sarah went quiet, then said Mom had been unconscious for hours before she passed, that no one's hand got squeezed.

I haven't slept properly in three days. The tissues on my nightstand keep piling up, and I can't seem to get out of bed before noon. My chest feels like someone's sitting on it. That memory was mine—the only good thing I had from the worst day of my life. Now it's just gone, evaporated like it never existed. Maybe it didn't.

story:
Jenny pushed the photo album away. "I don't understand. You said you hated that vacation."

Rachel frowned across the table. "What? No. That was the best summer of high school. We met those guys, went to all those beach parties."

"You cried every night." Jenny's voice came out smaller than she intended. "You told me you wanted to go home. I stayed because you needed me."

"Jenny, I think you're mixing it up with a different trip."

Jenny felt something crack inside her chest. She'd given up the art program for that trip—the one her teacher said she couldn't miss. She'd told herself for fifteen years that it was worth it, that Rachel had needed her. Her hands trembled as she closed the album. The room suddenly felt too small, the air too thin. She excused herself and locked herself in the bathroom, sliding down against the door.

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:

"The presentation failed because the client hated the concept," Wei said. "We stayed up all night redoing it, remember?"

Thomas shook his head slowly. "We stayed up because you deleted the file. I had to rebuild everything from scratch while you apologized."

Wei's face showed genuine confusion. "Tom, that never happened."

The weight in Thomas's stomach grew heavier. He'd carried guilt about that presentation for six years, believing he hadn't backed up Wei properly, that he'd let his friend take the fall alone. His eyes burned. He pressed his palms against them, elbows on the table. When he finally looked up, the fluorescent lights seemed too bright, everything sharp-edged and hostile. "I need some air," he whispered, and left his food untouched.

I thought bringing it up would make us laugh—remember when I defended you against Jake in tenth grade, got suspended for throwing that punch? We were supposed to be the friends who had each other's backs.

But Mia just blinked at me. "You didn't punch Jake. I did. You held me back, remember? Kept telling me it wasn't worth it."

The words hit me like cold water. I've been holding that memory like a trophy, proof that I wasn't always such a coward. My hands won't stop shaking. I keep scratching at my arms, a nervous habit I thought I'd broken. The apartment feels empty even with her sitting right there. I want to argue, to insist, but my voice has shrunk to nothing. What if everything I think I am is built on stories that never happened?

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:
Lisa pulled her cardigan tighter around herself despite the summer heat. "You're telling me I never sent you those letters? When you were in the hospital?"

Amber shook her head gently. "Lise, I never got anything from you. That's why I was so hurt. Radio silence for three months."

"But I wrote you every week." Lisa's voice had gone thin and distant. "I put them in the mailbox myself."

"Maybe they got lost?"

Lisa nodded mechanically, but inside she was collapsing. She'd spent twenty years believing Amber had simply never responded, that her words hadn't mattered enough. The betrayal she'd felt had become part of her identity. Now it was just... nothing. A postal error. Her fingers wouldn't stop twisting the cardigan fabric. She couldn't quite catch her breath. The park bench felt unsteady beneath her, or maybe that was just her.

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:
Omar stared at the ceiling of his childhood bedroom, phone still pressed to his ear. "Say that again."

His friend's voice crackled through: "Your dad showed up to your graduation, man. He was in the back. I saw him."

"He wasn't there, Jamal. I looked for him the whole time. That's why I—" Omar's voice cracked. He'd dropped out sophomore year of college, telling himself it didn't matter, that if Dad hadn't even showed up for high school graduation, why bother? The degree he never finished felt like a stone in his stomach. He'd built his entire identity around not caring, around expecting disappointment.

"I promise you, man. He was there."

Omar ended the call without saying goodbye. He lay very still, feeling like he'd been hollowed out. His eyes leaked silently, soaking the pillow. The darkness pressed down.

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:
"No, Charlie, you're wrong." My voice sounds distant even to me. "I drove you to the airport. We had that long conversation about your ex."

Charlie leans back, certain. "You were out of town. I took an Uber. I remember because the driver had an interesting accent and we talked the whole way."

I can feel my face getting hot, my vision blurring at the edges. I've told the story of that drive a hundred times—how I helped my best friend through his breakup, how I was there when it mattered. I wrote about it in my journal. It's in my therapist's notes as evidence that I'm not always absent, that I can show up for people.

My hands are trembling so badly I have to sit on them. The coffee shop suddenly feels too crowded, too loud. I can't seem to swallow properly. "I need to go," I say, and I'm already standing, already moving toward the door, my chest tight and my breathing shallow.

topic: Two friends realize they remember a shared event completely differently
story:
Patricia set down her wine glass with excessive care, as if any sudden movement might shatter her. "You're absolutely certain? I wasn't there when Robert proposed to you?"

"Patty, you were in Boston that weekend. You sent flowers afterward, remember?"

But Patricia remembered holding her friend's hand, remembered squealing with joy, remembered the restaurant's name and the way the light hit the ring. She'd told new acquaintances about being there for that moment, proof she was the kind of friend who showed up.

Her smile felt like it was carved from wood. "Right. Of course. The flowers." The wine suddenly tasted sour. She excused herself early, claiming a headache that wasn't entirely false. In her car, she sat in the parking lot for forty minutes, engine off, just staring at nothing. Her eyes felt raw. She couldn't make herself turn the key.

story:
David's shoulders had curled forward, making him look smaller somehow. "You really don't remember me visiting you every day after the accident?"

"Dave, you came once. Maybe twice." His brother's tone wasn't unkind, just matter-of-fact.

But David remembered. He remembered the smell of the hospital, the sound of the machines, the way he'd rearranged his entire schedule. Or thought he did. Now his memories felt like sand slipping through his fingers. He'd forgiven himself for so many other failures because at least he'd been there for this. At least he'd done this one thing right.

He nodded slowly, mechanically. His jaw ached from clenching. That hollow feeling spread through his chest, his arms, his legs. He couldn't quite focus his eyes. "Yeah. Sorry. I must be mixing things up." The words felt like stones in his mouth. He left before his brother could see his face crumple.

I'd been to the cemetery just yesterday.

topic: Someone receives flowers with no card attached

topic: Someone receives flowers with no card attached

topic: Someone receives flowers with no card attached

topic: Someone receives flowers with no card attached
story: Jasmine's hands moved mechanically as she unwrapped the red carnations. No card, no sender. She'd been moving through life like this for weeks—mechanical, automatic, hollow. Now she held flowers from a ghost, from no one, from someone. It didn't matter. Nothing seemed to matter much lately. She left them on the counter and went to draw a bath, the third one today, because at least in the water she didn't have to hold herself up.

topic: Someone receives flowers with no card attached
story: The lilies were waiting at reception when David came down. He'd been holed up in his hotel room for four days, leaving only when housekeeping insisted. He took them upstairs and sat on the edge of the bed, the flowers in his lap, staring at the wall where a mirror reflected a man who looked like him but older, grayer, somehow less substantial than before.

topic: Someone receives flowers with no card attached
